ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Augmenting Pseudo-Labels for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Train a weak teacher model on a randomly sampled subset of the web-crawl data, producing pseudo-labels for a larger subset of the data. Then, train a stronger student model on this pseudo-labeled data. Repeat the process with a new weak teacher to fine-tune the student. We will evaluate this method on its ability to automatically identify web pages with low quality (e.g. duplicated, noisy, non-relevant).
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments using approaches similar to DCLM and FineWeb-Edu without exploiting pseudo-labels.
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The method should result in improved data quality, as the pseudo-labels and fine-tuning process help to adapt the model to the web-crawl data's specific properties and provide a better starting point for more accurate data quality assessment. It might fail if the weak teacher model produces highly inaccurate pseudo-labels, which could lead to a weaker student model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Train a single model on multiple related tasks, such as (a) data quality classification (high-quality, low-quality), (b) language identification, and (c) task-specific relevance (e.g., relevant for a specific downstream task). We will use a shared encoder for all tasks and multiple task-specific decoders. This approach can help to leverage the relationships between tasks, improve the model's ability to generalize, and reduce overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare our multi-task learning approach to the single-task approaches used in existing work, such as training separate models for each task (DCLM, FineWeb-Edu).
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task learning approach should lead to improved generalization and performance across tasks, potentially resulting in better detection of low-quality web pages. It might fail if the relationships between tasks are too complex or if the shared encoder is not able to capture task-specific information effectively.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Leveraging Augmenting Pseudo-Labels for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Refine the previous proposal by incorporating an active learning component: select a subset of the pseudo-labeled data based on the teacher model's certainty (e.g., use uncertainty sampling) and have a human annotator validate the quality of the selected samples. Update the teacher model with the validated samples and repeat the process until convergence or a desired level of accuracy is achieved.
CONTROLS: Compare our refined method to the previous pseudo-labeling approach and evaluate the impact of active learning on data quality assessment performance.
COST: No change (estimated cost remains at 20,000 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The active learning component should help to improve the quality of the pseudo-labeled data and lead to more accurate data quality assessment. It might fail if the human annotator introduces bias or if the certainty-based sampling is not effective in selecting the most ambiguous samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weak Supervision from Multilingual Task Clustering
PROPOSAL: Identify clusters of multilingual tasks that share similar task-specific knowledge or vocabularies, such as document classification, sentiment analysis, or language translation. Use a small set of high-quality examples from each cluster as weak supervision to improve the data quality assessment model. We will leverage techniques such as k-means clustering or density-based clustering algorithms to identify these task clusters.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the data quality assessment model using the weak supervision derived from task clusters, and compare it to the performance using existing weak supervision approaches like DCLM and FineWeb-Edu.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The approach should lead to more robust data quality assessment by leveraging shared knowledge across related tasks. It might fail if the task clusters are poorly defined or if the shared knowledge is not transferable across tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Data Quality Assessment via Cross-Lingual Sentence Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Extract cross-lingual sentence embeddings using pre-trained multilingual language models (e.g., XLM-R, mBERT), and train a binary classifier to distinguish between high-quality and low-quality sentences based on the similarity between their embeddings. We will evaluate this approach's ability to transfer knowledge between languages and tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare our cross-lingual sentence embeddings approach to existing model-based data quality assessment methods, such as DCLM and FineWeb-Edu, and evaluate its performance on a variety of languages and tasks.
COST: 18,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The cross-lingual sentence embeddings approach should be able to generalize across languages and tasks, enabling more effective data quality assessment. It might fail if the pre-trained language models are not effective in capturing the nuances of linguistic styles or if the embeddings are not transferable across domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Transferability of Multilingual Data Quality Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of high-quality multilingual data quality models across different languages, domains, and downstream tasks. We will fine-tune pre-trained base models (e.g., sentence transformers) to the multilingual data quality task, and evaluate their performance on a range of languages and tasks. This will help identify areas where data quality models may generalize poorly and inform the development of more robust models.
CONTROLS: Compare the transferability of our multilingual data quality models to existing models, such as DCLM and FineWeb-Edu.
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The transferability analysis should reveal opportunities for fine-tuning pre-trained models and building more robust data quality models that can adapt to diverse languages and tasks. It might fail if the pre-trained models are not generalizable or if the data quality models are highly task-specific.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Leveraging Augmenting Pseudo-Labels for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Enhance the pseudo-labeling process by incorporating linguistic and domain-specific knowledge through the use of contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) and fine-tuning the teacher model on these embeddings for each language and task. This will enable the model to better capture content-specific and stylistic aspects of web pages, leading to improved data quality assessment.
CONTROLS: Compare our enhanced pseudo-labeling approach to the previous version without linguistic and domain-specific knowledge incorporation and evaluate the impact on data quality assessment performance.
COST: No change (estimated cost remains at 20,000 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The enhanced pseudo-labeling approach should lead to improved data quality by capturing more nuanced and language-specific characteristics of web pages. It might fail if the incorporation of linguistic and domain-specific knowledge is not effective or if the teacher model overfits to these new features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multilingual Data Quality Assessment via Neural Architecture Search
PROPOSAL: Apply neural architecture search (NAS) techniques to automatically discover the most effective neural network architectures for multilingual data quality assessment. We will use a range of architectures and search spaces, and evaluate their performance on a set of diverse multilingual tasks. This approach can help identify optimal architectures for specific languages, domains, and tasks, leading to improved data quality assessment performance and reduced computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare the NAS-optimized models to the existing models, such as DCLM and FineWeb-Edu, and evaluate their performance on a range of languages and tasks.
COST: 25,000 GPU-hours (note: NAS requires significant computational resources)
PREDICTION: The NAS-optimized models should lead to improved data quality assessment performance and adaptivity to diverse languages and tasks. It might fail if the search space is too large or if the NAS process converges to suboptimal architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pretraining and Fine-Tuning for Scalable Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of pretraining and fine-tuning large multilingual language models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R) for multilingual data quality assessment. We will pretrain the models on a large-scale multilingual corpus and fine-tune them on a range of data quality assessment tasks. This approach can help improve the robustness and scalability of data quality assessment models and enable efficient deployment on large datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of pretrained and fine-tuned models to existing models, such as DCLM and FineWeb-Edu, and evaluate their performance on a range of languages and tasks.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The pretraining and fine-tuning approach should lead to improved data quality assessment performance and scalability. It might fail if the pretraining process is not effective or if the fine-tuning process overfits to the data quality assessment tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Data Quality on Downstream Multilingual NLP Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of data quality on downstream multilingual NLP tasks, such as document classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. We will compare the performance of models trained on high-quality data versus low-quality data and evaluate the relationship between data quality and task performance. This study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the importance of data quality in multilingual NLP tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models trained on high-quality data to models trained on low-quality data, and evaluate the impact of data quality on a range of downstream tasks.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study should provide insights into the importance of data quality in multilingual NLP tasks and inform the development of more effective data quality assessment and correction strategies. It might fail if the data quality has a less significant impact on task performance than expected or if the results are not generalizable across tasks and languages.

CONTROLS: (1) baseline: existing heuristic-based deduplication and filtering techniques (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, etc.), (2) ablation study: compare专 lennt-changing evaluation criteria (e.g., using language-agnostic quality metrics), (3) validation on multilingual web-crawl data (e.g., CC-News).

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Language-Agnostic Quality Metrics on Model-Based Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate language-agnostic quality metrics for model-based data selection, such as using ranking or similarity-based evaluation criteria, to assess the quality of documents regardless of language.
CONTROLS: (1) propose 1 baseline model using language-specific quality metrics, (2) ablation study: compare coefficients or parameters between the language-specific and language-agnostic approaches, (3) validation on multilingual web-crawl data (e.g., CC-News).
COST: 500 GPU-hours (approximately 1 day with 400 GPUs).
PREDICTION: The language-agnostic approach may outperform the language-specific approach on certain languages or domains, but higher variance and increased risk of quality overestimation might occur due to broader quality criteria; result evaluation will require specific evaluation metrics for quality diversity.

TITLE: REVISED: Investigating the Impact of Language-Agnostic Quality Metrics on Model-Based Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a weighted ensemble model that combines language-specific and language-agnostic quality metrics, aimed at leveraging strengths from both approaches. The weights need to be learned from the auxiliary supervision data in each language. This approach may reduce the variance in quality judgments and improve overall evaluation consistency across languages.
CONTROLS: (1) ablation study: compare individual model performance on language-specific and language-agnostic metrics alone and their weighted combination, (2) validate on a split of the multilingual web-crawl data, e.g., CC-News, where one part is used for training and another for evaluation (set aside as before), (3) comparison against the initial baseline model.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (approximately 2 days with 400 GPUs).
PREDICTION: The weighted ensemble model may provide a better trade-off between language-specific and language-agnostic performance, but new hyperparameters will require careful tuning, and efficiency trade-offs in a web-scale setting might make it less feasible.
